title: The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress
authorsOrOrganization: Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, Ulrich Klocke
summary: An experimental study of interruptions during work reported that people often compensated by working faster after interruptions, while reporting greater stress, frustration, time pressure, and effort.
passages: Interrupted participants compensated by working faster, while reporting higher stress, frustration, time pressure, and effort.
limitations: A particular workplace task and setting; not a universal estimate for every person or notification.

title: The Attentional Cost of Receiving a Cell Phone Notification
authorsOrOrganization: Andrew K. Przybylski and Netta Weinstein
summary: Research examined whether mobile phone presence affects interpersonal conversation quality; it is relevant to device presence but should not be generalized to all focused work.
passages: The study tested mobile phone presence in a conversational setting, rather than measuring all forms of notification-driven work interruption.
limitations: The setting was conversation, not a direct test of every kind of study task or notification.

title: The Attentional Cost of Receiving a Cell Phone Notification
authorsOrOrganization: Andrew K. Przybylski and Netta Weinstein
summary: Phone presence may be relevant to social interaction, but this source alone cannot quantify the effect of notifications on an individual's productivity.
passages: Avoid interpreting one brief experiment as a diagnosis or stable personal attention trait.
limitations: Duplicate source topic retained as a separate practical framing; should be consolidated after source audit.

title: Task Switching and Cognitive Control
authorsOrOrganization: Joshua S. Rubinstein, David E. Meyer, Jeffrey E. Evans
summary: Experiments on task switching found measurable time costs when people switch between tasks, with costs depending on task and switching conditions.
passages: Switching between tasks can incur time costs; the size of the cost depends on the tasks and experimental conditions.
limitations: Laboratory task-switching results do not directly predict the exact cost of an individual's real-world phone checks.

title: The Distracted Mind: Ancient Brains in a High-Tech World
authorsOrOrganization: Adam Gazzaley and Larry D. Rosen; MIT Press
summary: A research-informed synthesis discusses limits of goal-directed cognition amid internal and external distraction.
passages: External interruptions and internal mind wandering can both compete with goal-directed activity.
limitations: A book-level synthesis rather than a single controlled trial; individual recommendations should be adapted.

title: Give Me a Break! A Meta-Analysis on the Efficacy of Breaks on Cognitive Functioning
summary: A meta-analysis examined break effects on cognitive performance and well-being, noting that effects vary by break type, duration, and outcome.
passages: Break benefits depend on the outcome measured and the type and duration of the break.
limitations: A break is not guaranteed to improve every task or every person; avoid a one-size-fits-all claim.

title: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement
authorsOrOrganization: Peter M. Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran
summary: Implementation intentions specify when, where, and how a goal-directed response will occur and have been studied as a goal-attainment strategy.
passages: An if-then plan can link a recognizable situation to a specific response, such as: if I reach for my phone, then I write down the urge and return to the next task step.
limitations: Effects vary by goal, context, and implementation; a plan is not a guarantee.

title: The Mere Presence of a Smartphone Reduces Baseline Cognitive Capacity
authorsOrOrganization: Adrian F. Ward, Kristen Duke, Ayelet Gneezy, Maarten W. Bos
summary: The authors reported experiments testing whether smartphone presence related to available cognitive capacity; subsequent work and debate mean claims should be cautious.
passages: The paper reports an association in its experimental settings; it should not be treated as a universal or uncontested effect size.
limitations: Specific experimental tasks and a debated literature; this local summary is not a full evidence review.

title: Cognitive Control in Media Multitasking
authorsOrOrganization: Eyal Ophir, Clifford Nass, Anthony D. Wagner
summary: Research investigated associations between media multitasking and cognitive control; the interpretation of individual differences should be cautious.
passages: Findings about media multitasking are not sufficient to diagnose a person or infer a stable personality trait.
limitations: Results and interpretations from a particular sample do not establish causal effects for all users.

title: The Limitations of Short Cognitive Tasks
summary: Brief tasks are influenced by task design, measurement noise, practice, and context; a short personal experiment is best treated as descriptive feedback.
passages: A short self-run experiment cannot establish a diagnosis, long-term change, or a person's stable attention ability.
limitations: This entry is intentionally marked unverified until the source page and metadata are checked during deployment or maintenance.
